previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a woman with a history of Addison’s disease and hypothyroidism, was admitted after a motor vehicle accident two days prior, during which she briefly lost consciousness and sustained a minor wrist burn. She developed a persistent bifrontal headache with photophobia, phonophobia, and vomiting, preventing her from taking her home steroid and thyroid medications. She was treated with IV fluids, IV hydrocortisone for adrenal coverage, and IV pain and anti-nausea medications. Her symptoms improved rapidly, and she was restarted on oral prednisone, Florinef, and Synthroid. Neurologic exams and repeat imaging were normal, supporting a diagnosis of migraine and post-concussion headache. She tolerated a regular diet, ambulated without issue, and was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to resume her baseline medications and monitor for worsening symptoms.

Brief Hospital Course:
*)Nausea/vomiting, malaise - in the setting of her history of 
Addison's disease and her electrolyte abnormalities, as well as 
symptoms similar to her prior presentations, she was admitted 
for management of likely adrenal crisis. Her blood pressure 
remained stable throughout her hospitalization. She was 
afebrile, and there was no evidence of infection as a 
precipitating event. After treatment with high-dose IV steroids, 
she felt much better and on the day of discharge her labs had 
markedly improved and she was able to eat and ambulate without 
difficulty. She was discharged on a rapid steroid taper, after a 
brief informal consultation of the Endocrinology fellow. She 
will have repeat labs drawn at her primary care doctor's office 
two days after discharge and will subsequently follow up with 
her endocrinologist. A message has been left with her primary 
care doctor to follow up her labs. 
.
*)Acute renal failure - on admission had an elevation of her 
creatinine to 1.8, which was thought to be pre-renal in etiology 
in the setting of her recent nausea/vomiting and decreased po 
intake. Her creatinine improved after IV fluids and was 1.2 on 
the day of discharge. She was to follow up with her 
endocrinologist, with repeat labs to be performed at that time.
.
*)Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo - on the day of admission 
experienced vertigo upon turning her head. Had had similar 
symptoms the prior year, but had not been evaluated due to other 
issues surrounding her recent surgery at that time. Symptoms at 
that time resolved spontaneously. She did not have any 
neurologic deficits on exam or history. ___ did not 
produce the classic nystagmus, but did seem to improve her 
symptoms. She was given instructions regarding Epley maneuvers, 
as well as precautions for calling her doctor or returning to 
the ED for any neurologic symptoms or persistent vertigo. On the 
day of discharge her symptoms had resolved and she was able to 
ambulate and perform other activities (i.e. knitting) without 
difficulty.
.
*)Hypertension - metoprolol was held during her hospitalization. 
While her blood pressures remained in the normal range, they 
were at the lower end of that range. She is to follow up at her 
primary care doctor's office in a few days for repeat labs; 
metoprolol may be re-started at that time, or on her visit with 
her endocrinologist. 
.
*)Hypothyroidism - her home dose of levothyroxine was continued.
.
*)Depression/anxiety - her home medications were continued.
.
